paragraphs: Auxiliary learning trains a model on additional tasks to improve its performance on a main task. This can help generalization, especially with small datasets, but creates a balancing problem: optimizing several objectives is harder, and an auxiliary task is useful only insofar as it helps the main objective.

The paper introduces AuxiNash, which treats this balancing problem as a bargaining game. Tasks have different bargaining powers, allowing them to exert unequal influence during learning. This asymmetry matches the purpose of auxiliary learning: the tasks contribute to a shared training process, but improving the main task remains the central goal.

AuxiNash learns those bargaining powers through an efficient procedure based on each task’s contribution to main-task performance. The authors derive convergence guarantees and report that the method consistently outperforms competing approaches across the multi-task benchmarks evaluated. Together, these results support adapting task influence according to its usefulness, giving the training procedure a principled way to decide how much assistance each auxiliary objective should provide.
icml-2023-auxiliary-learning-as-an-asymm.tldr: AuxiNash balances auxiliary tasks through an asymmetric bargaining game that learns how much each task should influence training.

paragraphs: Auxiliary Modality Learning uses additional kinds of input during training while requiring fewer kinds at test time. Its attraction is practical: a model can benefit from richer training information while reducing the inputs and overall computation needed when making predictions. The paper gives this setting a formal definition and organizes auxiliary modalities and model architectures in visual computing.

The authors also investigate when this approach works well, considering both optimization and the distributions of the data involved. This matters because the availability of an extra modality does not by itself establish how useful it will be. They propose a method to help select an auxiliary modality and estimate an upper bound on performance before carrying out auxiliary modality learning.

The paper then introduces a learning method based on generalized curriculum distillation, intended to make curriculum learning more effective. It reports the best performance among the state-of-the-art methods compared. The contribution therefore combines guidance about choosing auxiliary information with a concrete method for transferring its benefits into a model that uses fewer modalities at inference.
icml-2023-auxiliary-modality-learning-wi.tldr: The paper formalizes learning from extra training modalities and proposes modality selection and curriculum distillation methods.

paragraphs: Particle-based variational inference represents a Bayesian target distribution using a collection of particles that are updated during inference. Methods such as Stein variational gradient descent offer a scalable approach, but their behavior depends on settings such as the learning rate. Practitioners must tune that rate carefully to obtain suitable convergence toward the target distribution.

This paper introduces a family of particle-based inference methods built around coin betting. Their defining property is that they do not require a learning rate. The approach therefore addresses a specific source of manual tuning in gradient-based Bayesian inference while retaining the particle-based setting used by established scalable methods.

The authors evaluate their methods through numerical examples that include high-dimensional models and datasets. They report performance comparable to other particle-based variational inference algorithms without needing learning-rate tuning. The stated benefit is thus competitive inference with one important tuning burden removed. The evidence supports that comparison on the examples studied; the abstract does not claim that the methods eliminate every other modeling or configuration choice.
icml-2023-coin-sampling-gradient-based-b.tldr: Coin-betting-based particle methods perform Bayesian inference without learning rates and achieve comparable performance in the reported examples.

paragraphs: Learning with discrete random choices often requires estimating how an expected outcome changes when the sampling distribution changes. Gumbel-Softmax estimators address this using a relaxation controlled by a temperature parameter. The Gumbel-Rao estimator adds internal sampling to reduce variability in the gradient estimate, but that extra sampling can be computationally costly.

The authors analyze what happens as its temperature approaches zero. They show that the estimator has a limit with a simple closed-form expression, which they call ZGR. This limiting estimator is inexpensive and easy to implement, with favorable bias and variance properties. Its simplicity makes the mathematical limit useful as a practical estimator.

ZGR also has an unexpected structure: it averages the straight-through and DARN estimators, even though those two estimators perform relatively poorly individually. The authors report that the ST–ZGR family practically dominates the Gumbel-Rao family in bias–variance tradeoffs and outperforms state-of-the-art unbiased estimators. The findings show how analyzing a limiting case can produce a simpler computational method with strong empirical tradeoffs.
icml-2023-cold-analysis-of-rao-blackwell.tldr: Analyzing Gumbel-Rao at zero temperature yields a simple, inexpensive gradient estimator with favorable reported bias–variance tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Cooperative agents can train centrally while making decisions separately, but changing team compositions complicate what each agent can observe. An agent with a broad view may focus on irrelevant surroundings, while an agent with a narrow view may miss teammates. The paper addresses both sources of difficulty in maintaining cooperation.

CAMA divides input entities according to their contribution and applies complementary attention mechanisms. For highly contributing entities, it strengthens attention using a representation tied to action execution. That representation is obtained through action prediction with an inverse model, helping connect attention to behavior that matters for the agent’s decisions.

For entities contributing less, CAMA uses a conditional mutual information estimator to compress information into brief messages. This mechanism is intended to support cooperation beyond an agent’s immediate observation range. The authors report strong results on StarCraftII, MPE, and Traffic Junction, supporting their claim of more stable, sustained teamwork. The method’s central idea is to address distracting observations and missing observations together, through selective emphasis and compact communication.
icml-2023-complementary-attention-for-mu.tldr: CAMA combines action-related attention and compact messages to help cooperative agents handle distracting and incomplete observations.

paragraphs: Large pretrained models have made fine-tuning effective in vision and language, but many other modalities lack suitable pretrained models. ORCA addresses this gap by adapting a single large pretrained model to tasks across diverse input modalities. The aim is to make existing pretrained knowledge useful in settings where a directly relevant model is unavailable.

Its workflow has two stages. First, an embedding network learns to transform the target inputs so their feature distribution aligns with the modality used in pretraining. The pretrained model is then fine-tuned on those embedded inputs. Alignment prepares the new data for the model, while refinement adapts the combined system to the target task.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks covering more than 60 datasets and 12 modalities, outperforming a broad range of compared approaches. Ablation studies highlight the importance of alignment, and experiments demonstrate usefulness when data is limited. These findings support distribution alignment as an important step in making cross-modal transfer effective across the evaluated tasks.
icml-2023-cross-modal-fine-tuning-align-.tldr: ORCA adapts pretrained models across modalities by first aligning input features and then fine-tuning on the transformed data.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems use user vectors to retrieve relevant items, and multiple vectors can represent a person’s different interests. Having several interests represented, however, leaves another question: how much should each interest influence the recommendations now? The paper argues that existing approaches can miss these preferences or assume that every interest fades at the same rate.

The Multi-Interest Preference model uses a user’s sequence of engagement to construct multiple interest representations and learn a weight for each one. Those weights express the user’s relative preference across the representations. Retrieval then draws candidates from the different interests proportionally, connecting the learned preferences directly to which items enter the candidate set.

This approach matters because identifying a topic of interest and deciding how strongly to prioritize it are separate parts of recommendation. MIP models both within its retrieval approach, using sequential behavior more effectively. Experiments on several industrial-scale datasets demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The reported evidence supports weighted multi-interest retrieval without establishing that all users’ interests follow a single shared pattern of change.
icml-2023-everyones-preference-changes-d.tldr: MIP learns multiple user interests and their relative weights so recommendation candidates can be retrieved in proportion to user preferences.

paragraphs: Model explanations are often built from different heuristics, making their underlying assumptions difficult to compare. This paper places interpretability within statistical inference by introducing a general probabilistic model for interpretable predictions. Its parameters can be fitted by maximum likelihood, and the framework is designed to accommodate any predictor architecture and prediction problem.

A neural network acts as a selector, allowing explanations to be produced quickly at inference time. The authors show that several popular explanation methods arise as special cases of regularized maximum-likelihood fitting within this framework. That connection gives seemingly different methods a shared mathematical basis and makes it possible to examine problems they have in common.

One shared issue is imputation: how to fill in information that a selection leaves out. The authors introduce datasets with known ground-truth selections so that feature-importance maps can be evaluated against an explicit reference. Their experiments find that multiple imputation produces more reasonable interpretations. The result emphasizes that an explanation depends on both the selected information and how the remaining information is handled.
icml-2023-explainability-as-statistical-.tldr: A probabilistic framework unifies explanation methods and identifies imputation as an important influence on interpretation quality.

paragraphs: FlexGen targets language-model workloads where many requests can be processed in batches and individual response latency is less important. Large models strain GPU memory, so the system combines resources from the GPU, CPU, and disk. Its objective is high total generation throughput under limited hardware resources.

The engine solves a linear programming problem to choose efficient patterns for storing and accessing tensors. It also compresses model weights and the attention cache to four bits, with negligible reported accuracy loss. Together, these mechanisms expand the available batch-size choices, allowing the system to increase its maximum throughput despite limited GPU memory.

For OPT-175B on a single 16GB GPU, the authors report one generated token per second with an effective batch size of 144, substantially exceeding the compared offloading systems. They also benchmark a 30B model on seven representative HELM sub-scenarios in 21 hours using a 16GB GPU. These results concern batched, latency-insensitive work and demonstrate how coordinated memory placement and compression can make large-model inference practical with limited GPU resources.
icml-2023-flexgen-high-throughput-genera.tldr: FlexGen increases batched LLM inference throughput on a single GPU by coordinating GPU, CPU, and disk resources and compressing tensors.

paragraphs: Autoencoders learn compressed representations, but even shallow nonlinear versions raise basic questions about their best possible performance and what gradient training learns. This paper studies two-layer autoencoders in the proportional regime, where input dimension grows linearly with representation size. That setting addresses a gap left by analyses of linear models or regimes with vanishing or diverging compression rates.

The authors characterize the solutions that minimize population risk and show that gradient methods achieve those minimizers. They also describe the structure of the minimizing solutions, connecting optimal performance to the features learned during training. This links questions about what the architecture can achieve with questions about what optimization actually finds.

For sign activation functions, the analysis establishes fundamental limits for lossy compression of Gaussian sources using shallow autoencoders. The proofs apply to Gaussian data. Numerical simulations on standard datasets show behavior consistent with the theoretical predictions beyond that setting, providing empirical evidence of universality while leaving the formal guarantees tied to the stated Gaussian assumptions.
icml-2023-fundamental-limits-of-two-laye.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal nonlinear two-layer autoencoders for Gaussian data and shows that gradient methods reach those solutions.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning with linear function approximation when costs can change adversarially. The learner faces unknown environment dynamics and bandit feedback, so it must act without either a known transition model or full information about costs. This is a harder setting than versions that assume full feedback or favorable exploration conditions.

The proposed policy optimization algorithm combines mirror descent with least-squares policy evaluation. An auxiliary Markov decision process is used to compute exploration bonuses, bringing exploration into the policy-update procedure. The authors establish computational efficiency alongside a regret guarantee, addressing both the algorithm’s ability to run efficiently and its cumulative learning performance.

For this general setting, the regret bound improves from a previous rate of order K^(14/15) to K^(6/7), with logarithmic factors suppressed. A second version assumes access to an environment simulator and achieves a bound of order K^(2/3), again suppressing logarithmic factors. That stronger result depends on simulator access, while requiring no additional exploratory assumptions. The contribution is therefore improved theoretical performance under two explicitly different information settings.
icml-2023-improved-regret-for-efficient-.tldr: An efficient policy optimization algorithm improves regret bounds for linear reinforcement learning with adversarial costs and limited feedback.

paragraphs: A model may solve a reasoning problem when every supplied detail is useful yet struggle when the same kind of task includes unrelated information. This paper investigates that sensitivity to irrelevant context. It focuses on an evaluation gap: many existing benchmarks primarily present inputs whose information is relevant to the task.

The authors introduce Grade-School Math with Irrelevant Context, or GSM-IC, an arithmetic reasoning dataset that includes unnecessary information in problem descriptions. They use it to compare the distractibility of different prompting techniques. The evaluation asks whether a model can identify and use the information needed for a calculation while disregarding other details.

The results show that irrelevant information can readily distract the evaluated language models. The paper also identifies ways to reduce this problem, including self-consistency decoding and an explicit instruction to ignore irrelevant context. These are reported as mitigations. The broader significance is that reasoning performance depends partly on selecting relevant information, so success on clean problem descriptions does not fully capture the behavior tested by GSM-IC.
icml-2023-large-language-models-can-be-e.tldr: GSM-IC shows that irrelevant context can disrupt language-model arithmetic reasoning, while certain prompting and decoding approaches mitigate the problem.

paragraphs: Different learning algorithms can produce models that use information differently. This paper makes that comparison concrete by asking which input transformations distinguish their behavior. A distinguishing transformation changes the predictions of models trained with one algorithm while leaving those trained with another unaffected. This turns a broad comparison into a specific behavioral question.

ModelDiff approaches the problem through the datamodels framework, comparing learning algorithms according to how their resulting models use training data. The connection to training data gives the comparison an organizing principle: differences in learned behavior are examined through the examples used to produce that behavior. The goal is to identify meaningful differences between training procedures.

The authors demonstrate the framework in three case studies: training with or without data augmentation, with or without pretraining, and with different stochastic gradient descent hyperparameters. These examples span changes to the data, the starting model, and the optimization process. They illustrate ModelDiff as a tool for investigating how training choices alter model behavior, rather than establishing one training choice as universally preferable.
icml-2023-modeldiff-a-framework-for-comp.tldr: ModelDiff compares learning algorithms through their use of training data and input transformations that distinguish their models’ predictions.

paragraphs: Multiple cameras give a robot richer observations, but their value can extend to learning better internal representations. This paper investigates that use of multiple views for visual manipulation. It trains a masked autoencoder to reconstruct pixels from randomly masked viewpoints, making reconstruction across views part of the representation-learning task.

A world model is then learned using the autoencoder’s representations. The authors demonstrate the approach both when control uses multiple views and when control uses only one view, with extra cameras contributing during representation learning. The latter setting shows that additional cameras can help shape the learned representation even when they are not all used for control.

The paper also trains the autoencoder with randomized viewpoints, enabling policy training under strong viewpoint randomization. The resulting policy transfers to real-robot tasks without camera calibration or an adaptation procedure in the demonstrated setting. These findings connect multi-view reconstruction with flexibility in camera placement: learning from varied perspectives can support policies that work across the viewpoint changes evaluated by the authors.
icml-2023-multi-view-masked-world-models.tldr: Multi-view masked reconstruction learns representations that support robotic control and demonstrated real-robot transfer without camera calibration or adaptation.

paragraphs: TimeDiff adapts denoising diffusion to time-series prediction using a non-autoregressive forecasting model. The paper focuses on how to condition the model effectively, introducing two mechanisms that connect diffusion-based prediction to the structure of time-series data. These mechanisms are future mixup and autoregressive initialization.

Future mixup uses parts of the ground-truth future as conditioning information during learning, in a manner similar to teacher forcing. Autoregressive initialization supplies an initial prediction containing basic time-series patterns, such as short-term trends. The two mechanisms serve different purposes: one enriches the learning signal, while the other provides a more informed starting point for prediction.

The authors evaluate TimeDiff on nine real-world datasets. They report consistent improvements over existing time-series diffusion models and the best overall performance across a wider group of strong baselines, including transformers and FiLM. These results support the value of the proposed conditioning design for the evaluated forecasting tasks. The model remains non-autoregressive despite using an autoregressive component for initialization, so that component’s role is specifically to help establish the starting forecast.
icml-2023-non-autoregressive-conditional.tldr: TimeDiff improves diffusion-based forecasting with future mixup and autoregressive initialization, achieving strong results across nine datasets.

paragraphs: Multi-source-free domain adaptation learns a target model using existing source models without accessing their original training data. That restriction matters when privacy or storage constraints make source datasets unavailable. Existing approaches commonly use source models to assign pseudo-labels to target data, then train a new model from those generated labels.

This paper examines the underlying limits of that process through an information-theoretic bound on target-model generalization error. The bound exposes a bias–variance tradeoff, giving a theoretical basis for reasoning about adaptation quality. The authors use it to study three choices: how to aggregate source domains, which pseudo-labels to select, and how to align features jointly.

Those insights lead to new algorithms designed to balance the tradeoff. Experiments on multiple datasets support the analysis and show state-of-the-art performance for the proposed algorithm, particularly on challenging datasets including Office-Home and DomainNet. The contribution links practical adaptation decisions to a generalization analysis, providing a rationale for how source-model information should be combined and used when the underlying source data cannot be revisited.
icml-2023-on-balancing-bias-and-variance.tldr: An information-theoretic bias–variance analysis guides improved domain adaptation using source models without their training data.

paragraphs: Many generative models learn a prescribed probability path from noise to data. This paper studies how to choose such a path within the Gaussian family, which includes diffusion paths. It focuses on minimizing kinetic energy, a criterion associated with simpler particle trajectories, easier sampling, and empirical improvements in generation quality and unseen-data likelihood.

The authors show that kinetic energy simplifies so that the data enters through one scalar function, called the data separation function. They characterize optimal paths using a one-dimensional ordinary differential equation. They also approximate data-dependent optimal paths by estimating that function and minimizing the resulting kinetic energy.

A key theorem concerns normalized datasets with n samples in d dimensions: the separation function approaches one as n divided by the square root of d approaches zero. Consequently, the Conditional Optimal Transport path becomes kinetic optimal in that limit. Experiments on ImageNet support the theory. The optimality claim is therefore tied to the stated asymptotic regime, while the broader framework offers a way to investigate data-dependent paths.
icml-2023-on-kinetic-optimal-probability.tldr: The paper reduces kinetic-optimal Gaussian path design to a scalar function and proves Conditional Optimal Transport becomes optimal in a specified limit.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves an optimization problem whose solution depends on another, lower-level optimization problem. It appears in hyperparameter tuning, meta-learning, and reinforcement learning. The nested structure makes computation difficult, and much prior progress on scalable algorithms has focused on lower-level problems that are strongly convex or have no constraints.

This paper approaches the nested problem through a penalty formulation. The authors show that, under certain conditions, solving the reformulated problem recovers solutions of the original bilevel problem. That qualification is central: the result establishes when the reformulation preserves the desired solutions, rather than claiming that any penalty construction will do so.

They then propose penalty-based bilevel gradient descent and prove finite-time convergence for a constrained bilevel setting without requiring lower-level strong convexity. Experiments demonstrate the algorithm’s efficiency. The contribution extends the analyzed setting to constrained lower-level problems beyond the strong-convexity requirement, while connecting the algorithm to a conditional justification for its penalty formulation. This supplies both a computational approach and theoretical support for the class of problems studied.
icml-2023-on-penalty-based-bilevel-gradi.tldr: A penalty-based gradient method has finite-time convergence guarantees for constrained bilevel optimization without lower-level strong convexity.

paragraphs: Random Edge Coding is a one-shot method for compressing large labeled graphs. It uses bits-back coding to sample edges and vertices without replacement from an edge list while preserving graph structure. The method connects graph compression to random graph models with symmetries in how edges and their endpoints are ordered.

When paired with a parameter-free model based on Pólya’s Urn, its worst-case computation grows quasi-linearly with the number of observed edges, while memory grows linearly. It also uses only integer arithmetic. These properties make the method particularly suitable for sparse graphs, where the observed edge count is the important quantity governing its resource requirements.

The authors prove optimality for a class of random graph models unchanged by permutations of edges or by swapping vertices within an edge. That model class defines the scope of the optimality result. Experiments show competitive compression on real-world network datasets and scaling to millions of nodes and edges. Together, the theory and experiments support a compression method that combines structure-preserving coding with practical large-graph efficiency.
icml-2023-one-shot-compression-of-large-.tldr: Random Edge Coding efficiently compresses large graphs using bits-back coding, with optimality proved for a specified class of symmetric graph models.

paragraphs: Time-series signals can contain corresponding events at different times, making even averaging difficult before alignment. Diffeomorphic Temporal Alignment Nets address this using learned temporal transformations and a shared alignment model. Existing formulations, however, depend heavily on regularization settings whose best values vary by dataset and often require extensive experimental search.

The paper introduces a regularization-free formulation built around a new objective called Inverse Consistency Averaging Error, or ICAE, along with a related triplet loss. The goal is to make the alignment objective itself behave well enough to remove dependence on the regularization term. This directly targets the costly search for dataset-specific regularization hyperparameters.

Experiments across 128 UCR datasets show the proposed approach outperforming contemporary methods despite omitting regularization. ICAE also enables the first DTAN supporting variable-length signals, extending the kinds of inputs the framework can align. The findings connect a change in the training objective to two practical benefits: avoiding the stated regularization search and accommodating signals that need not all have the same length.
icml-2023-regularization-free-diffeomorp.tldr: A new alignment loss removes DTAN’s dependence on regularization tuning and enables support for variable-length signals.

paragraphs: Sequential changepoint detection asks whether a property of a data-generating distribution has changed as observations arrive. This paper connects that problem to sequential estimation. Its central result says that if a confidence sequence can be constructed for the parameter or functional of interest, it can also be used to perform changepoint detection for that quantity.

The detector compares two confidence sequences, one running forward and one constructed by reversing time. It signals a change when the two no longer intersect. The logic is that their sets of plausible values have become incompatible. The backward confidence sequence is itself a new construction that the authors suggest may have uses beyond this detector.

This reduction matters because advances in confidence-sequence methods can translate into methods for detecting changes in the same quantities. The authors provide nonasymptotic guarantees for false-alarm frequency and detection delay, and demonstrate numerical effectiveness on several problems. The result is conditional on being able to construct the relevant confidence sequence, giving an explicit route from an estimation tool to a detection procedure.
icml-2023-sequential-changepoint-detecti.tldr: Comparing forward and backward confidence sequences turns sequential estimation tools into changepoint detectors with finite-sample guarantees.

paragraphs: Step-by-step demonstrations can help language models solve reasoning tasks, but their usefulness depends on the examples supplied. Creating many high-quality demonstrations by hand is expensive. Synthetic prompting starts with a few handcrafted examples, uses the model to generate additional examples, and selects effective demonstrations for later reasoning prompts.

Generation alternates between backward and forward processes. In the backward process, the model produces a question that matches a sampled reasoning chain, with the aim of making the question clear and solvable. In the forward process, it develops a more detailed reasoning chain for that question. The two directions connect question construction with improvement of the corresponding explanation.

The authors evaluate the method on numerical, symbolic, and algorithmic reasoning tasks and report improvements over existing prompting techniques. The contribution is a way to expand a small collection of manually written demonstrations while working on the quality of the generated question-and-reasoning pairs. Its reported success supports using synthetic examples and selection to improve prompting across the tested reasoning categories.
icml-2023-synthetic-prompting-generating.tldr: Synthetic prompting expands a few handcrafted examples through alternating question generation and reasoning refinement, then selects useful demonstrations.

paragraphs: An agent learning sequential decisions may have both rewards and a teacher that can recommend actions. Each source has weaknesses. Reward-based learning can require substantial data, especially with sparse rewards or partial observability. A teacher may be suboptimal, or may use privileged information that the agent cannot observe and therefore cannot reliably imitate.

TGRL addresses the decision of how much to follow the teacher and how much to learn from rewards. Earlier combined approaches balanced imitation and reinforcement learning through heuristics and problem-specific tuning. The paper proposes a principled method that adjusts this balance dynamically, allowing the two supervision sources to play different roles during learning.

The authors report that TGRL outperforms strong baselines across diverse domains without hyperparameter tuning. The significance is tied to the stated setting: teacher guidance is available, but its usefulness may be limited by information differences or imperfect actions. Dynamically balancing guidance and reward learning provides a way to benefit from teaching while accounting for those reasons that imitation alone may fall short.
icml-2023-tgrl-an-algorithm-for-teacher-.tldr: TGRL dynamically balances teacher imitation and reward-based learning, outperforming strong baselines across the reported domains without hyperparameter tuning.

paragraphs: Gradient-based value estimation in reinforcement learning offers favorable stability properties, but often learns much more slowly than temporal-difference methods. This paper investigates the cause of that gap. It shows that the mean square Bellman error is poorly conditioned: its Hessian has a large condition number, creating an unfavorable optimization landscape for gradient-based updates.

The proposed remedy is a low-complexity proximal method that works without batches and approximately follows a Gauss–Newton direction. Its main algorithm, RANS, changes the update direction to address the conditioning problem. The method is also asymptotically robust to parameterization, linking its long-run behavior to the way the estimation problem is represented.

The authors report that RANS is significantly faster than residual-gradient methods while having almost the same computational complexity. On the classic problems tested, it is competitive with temporal-difference learning. These findings suggest that better handling the geometry of the Bellman-error objective can improve learning speed without a comparable increase in computational cost, while the comparison with temporal-difference methods remains specific to the evaluated problems.
icml-2023-toward-efficient-gradient-base.tldr: RANS accelerates gradient-based value estimation by approximately following Gauss–Newton directions to address poor Bellman-error conditioning.

paragraphs: GFlowNets learn to generate discrete objects with probabilities proportional to their nonnegative rewards. Their objectives guarantee the desired distribution when the loss is globally minimized across all states or trajectories. This paper investigates what happens under practical training limits, where that ideal optimization condition may not be achieved.

The authors introduce an efficient way to compare the learned sampling distribution with the target reward distribution. They also explain why learned flows matter for generalization: the training data can leave those flows underdetermined. Consequently, the way a model resolves that freedom affects how closely its generated objects follow the desired reward-weighted distribution.

To improve training, the paper proposes prioritized replay of high-reward objects, relative edge-flow policy parameterization, and a guided trajectory-balance objective. It shows how the guided objective can address credit assignment to substructures and reports substantial improvements in sample efficiency on biochemical design tasks. The contribution connects a practical evaluation method with training changes intended to improve distribution matching when available learning resources are limited.
icml-2023-towards-understanding-and-impr.tldr: The paper analyzes practical GFlowNet distribution matching and introduces training changes that substantially improve sample efficiency on biochemical design tasks.
